title: Patch: a ruling's proof must be a test that can run

# #1718: Patch: a ruling's proof must be a test that can run
Opened by @jgoetzmann-bot.

## What it actually means

Every game ruling names the tests that prove it, and a repository check enforces that pairing. Today the check only asks whether a matching *name* appears in the file — a skipped test, or a helper function that is never registered as a test, counts as proof all the same. A ruling can therefore claim evidence nobody runs, and nobody notices. After the change, only a test that can actually execute counts; skipping or demoting a proof fails the check.

## Why

`spec check`'s `proves()` (`crates/tools/src/spec.rs:739-793`) collects a Rust `fn`/`mod` name or a TypeScript `it(`/`test(`/`describe(` title and never records attributes: its own fixture credits `it.skip('R5 skipped', …)` as a proof of R5 (:1131-1146), and a plain `fn r58_helper` never marked `#[test]` would pass the same way (:1103-1116). CLAUDE.md rule 3 ties every ruling to its proving test; the current check verifies a name exists, not that a test runs — a skipped or refactored-away proof keeps the index green while coverage quietly disappears.

## Proposal

Tighten both collectors: a Rust item must carry `#[test]`/`#[tokio::test]` or a `daily:`-reasoned `#[ignore]`, or be a `mod` inside `#[cfg(test)]`; a TypeScript title under `.skip`, `.todo`, `.fixme` or `.only` does not count. SQL `\echo` evidence headings are unchanged.

## Where it lands

`crates/tools/src/spec.rs` (attribute and modifier tracking in `rust_item_names`/`ts_test_titles`) plus its unit tests; any current `proven_in` entries that turn out non-executable get fixed in the same change.

## Acceptance criteria

- The fixture cases above flip: skipped tests and plain functions no longer satisfy `proven_in`.
- `cargo jackioh spec check` passes on the real tree — or the change fixes the few proofs it exposes.
- `daily:`-ignored tests still count (they run in `super.yml`, so they are executable proof).

## Size and risks

Medium: attribute/modifier tracking in two small parsers plus the policy for `mod` and SQL cases. Risk is surfacing a handful of currently-accepted weak proofs — which is the point.
